name: Probiotics for acne
lead: Probiotics are live microorganisms intended to confer a health benefit, sold as supplements, in fermented foods and in some topical products [1]. For acne, oral and topical probiotics are discussed on the basis of the proposed gut-skin axis and of the skin's own microbial community [2][3].

Published reviews describe the research as preliminary. A review summarised in Wikipedia describes probiotics and synbiotics as showing early potential to reduce inflammatory acne lesions and improve skin barrier function [1]. Several systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised trials of oral probiotics were published in 2025 [4][5][6]. Benefits of probiotics are generally strain-specific, so results do not transfer between products [1].
infobox: Gut-skin axis; skin microbiome modulation; reduced inflammation
Dietary supplements (US); EU bans the word on labels [1]

paras: Acne involves abnormal keratinisation of the sebaceous duct, colonisation by Cutibacterium acnes, raised sebum production and hormonal factors, and treatment can be long and affect quality of life [3]. Researchers have proposed that the gut microbiota influences these processes, which is the basis for oral probiotic use [3].

Laboratory work has also examined the skin microbiome. A 2014 study reported that Staphylococcus epidermidis can ferment glycerol in ways that inhibit growth of C. acnes, and suggested implications for probiotic treatment [7]. Reviews of the cutaneous microbiota describe dysbiosis as contributing to acne [8]. Diet is another suspected influence, and a 2021 review discusses glycemic load and acne [9].

A scoping review (2025) examined probiotic supplements and topical applications for acne [10], a 2013 article reviewed probiotics in acne and rosacea [11], and a 2022 narrative review covered the microbiome and probiotics in acne vulgaris [3]. Meta-analyses of randomised trials of oral probiotics were published in 2025 in Cureus, Medicina and Clinical and Experimental Dermatology [4][5][6]; their individual findings are not summarised here.

Trial registrations show a range of designs: an oral probiotic added to benzoyl peroxide plus adapalene (n=400, phase 4) [12], probiotics compared with azithromycin (n=75) and combined with azithromycin (n=60) [13][14], a topical probiotic cream study (n=20) [15], and trials of oral probiotics against placebo in patients with moderate acne [16][17]. A trial of probiotics and skin hydration in youth with mild acne has been completed [18]. Registration entries do not report outcomes in the material reviewed.

Probiotics are generally considered safe, but immunocompromised people, premature infants and people with central venous catheters or heart valve disease may face higher risks, and bloodstream infections have been rarely reported [1]. The European Food Safety Authority has rejected commercial probiotic health claim petitions for insufficient evidence, and the US FDA and FTC have issued warning letters over disease claims [1].
A 2026 study reported on Lactobacillus-derived extracellular vesicles as a multi-target acne approach in laboratory research [19].

card.summary: Gut-skin axis supplements and creams for acne; reviews and trials exist, but evidence is preliminary and strain-specific.
card.note: Benefits are strain-specific; higher infection risk in immunocompromised people.

quick.overview:
Probiotics are live bacteria sold as capsules, foods or skin products. For acne they are used on the idea that gut or skin microbes influence breakouts.

Several meta-analyses of randomised trials appeared in 2025, and reviews describe the evidence as preliminary.
quick.mechanism: Proposed routes are the gut-skin axis (gut microbes affecting inflammation and hormones) and shifts in skin bacteria such as C. acnes. A lab study found skin S. epidermidis can inhibit C. acnes via fermentation.
quick.risks: Probiotics are generally considered safe, but rare bloodstream infections have occurred in immunocompromised or critically ill people. Effects are strain-specific, and regulators such as EFSA have rejected probiotic health claims for insufficient evidence.
